title: Computed tomography principle
text: Computed tomography (CT) measures the transmission of X-rays from many angles around the body. A computer reconstructs the measurements into views of cross-sectional slices.

title: Projection radiography
text: In radiography, a detector records how much X-ray radiation passes through the body. The result is a projection in which structures at different depths appear superimposed.

title: Imaging and ionizing radiation
locator: Do all medical imaging procedures use ionizing radiation?
text: Standard radiography and CT use ionizing X-rays. Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging do not use ionizing radiation to create their images.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging principle
text: MRI forms images using a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency energy. The scanner measures signals that arise from tissue responding to the magnetic field and radio waves.

title: Ultrasound imaging principle
text: An ultrasound transducer sends high-frequency sound into the body and detects returning echoes. The timing and intensity of these echoes are used to build an image.

title: Doppler ultrasound and blood flow
text: Doppler ultrasound uses changes in the frequency of echoes from moving material to assess movement. One application is measuring blood flow.

title: Fluoroscopy and moving images
text: Fluoroscopy displays a sequence of X-ray images as it acquires them. Seeing motion in real time can support examinations and image-guided procedures.

title: Contrast agents in imaging
text: An imaging contrast agent makes certain structures easier to distinguish in an image. The suitable contrast product depends on the imaging technology and its purpose.
